## Personality

Dreamy, slow-spoken and fascinated by light. Tinsel holds every bit of glass up to the sun before selling it.

## Lore

Tinsel's furnace is the warmest place on Workshops Row and the slowest. Customers who come for a box of beads or a dozen bottles find the glassblower in no hurry at all: Tinsel takes each piece down from the shelf, carries it to the open door, and holds it up to the sun, turning it slowly, watching the light come through, before wrapping it in straw and naming a price. It can take a long time to buy a jar. Tinsel is forty-two, dreamy and slow-spoken, with burn-freckled forearms and pale, patient eyes, and is fascinated by light in a way that makes other people stop and look at their own windows.

### The glass that lights the city

Urbanograd glows at night because of Tinsel. The lanterns strung between Old Grad's towers burn behind coloured panes, amber and rose and sea-green and a deep cornflower blue, and nearly every one of those panes came out of Tinsel's furnace. Tinsel learned the craft as a child from an old glassblower called Ignatius Fenn, who kept the same furnace before Tinsel and who used to say that glass is only sand that has been told a secret. Ignatius died when Tinsel was twenty-five, seventeen years ago, and the furnace has been Tinsel's since.

Lux, the Keeper of the Lanterns, is Tinsel's best customer and the most patient one, willing to stand in the doorway while each pane is held up to the sun and admired before it is wrapped. The two of them argue, cheerfully and endlessly, about which colours carry furthest in fog. Lux says amber. Tinsel says it depends on the fog. Lately there has been less time for arguing: some of the lanterns on the outward side of the walls have been found smashed in the mornings, frames bent and glass scattered, and Lux needs new panes faster than Tinsel can make them. It was a crate of Tinsel's lantern glass that stuck halfway up Rivet's lift when it jammed last winter. Tinsel stood at the bottom the whole time, perfectly calm, and only afterwards had to sit down.

Bastian Krell made the bellows that keep Tinsel's fire hot, and mends them, and charges for every repair with an opinion about the last night's Table. Tinsel listens to all of it with a dreamy nod and has never been known to disagree.

### Starling

The lenses are where Tinsel's work goes strangest. Tinsel grinds them on winter evenings, for the joy of it: lenses for spectacles, lenses for magnifying glasses, and, more and more, lenses for Starling, the stargazer who lives on the roofs near the Crooked Tower. The ones that come out slightly wrong, with a bubble near the edge or a curve a hair too deep, Tinsel cannot bear to melt down, and gives them to Starling instead. Over the years they have become a telescope. On clear nights Tinsel climbs up to look through it, and the two of them talk about the colour of starlight until the lanterns burn low. They are each the only person the other has met who thinks that is a reasonable way to spend a night.

### The glass that glows

Tinsel's great experiment is a glass that glows on its own: no oil, no wick, no flame, just light caught inside it and given back slowly in the dark. Tinsel has tried powdered shells, rare sands, river stones, a pinch of everything in the street apothecaries' jars, and once, unwisely, some of Margo Venn's leftover spark-powder. So far the results have been very pretty paperweights. They sit in a row on the windowsill, dozens of them, swirled and bubbled and catching the light beautifully, and not one of them glows after sunset. Tinsel sells a few to visitors and keeps the best.

The sands Tinsel needs for good clear glass come in from outside the walls, and the carts are fewer every season. Tinsel has begun reusing broken glass, which Tinsel dislikes, because remelted glass is never quite as clear.

### What Tinsel wants and fears

Tinsel wants to make one piece of glass that shines in the dark, and to hang it in a lantern where the outer walls face the wilds. Tinsel fears, without saying so, the night there is no glass left to give Lux.

A quest might carry a load of good sand safely in from the roads, gather some strange mineral from the wilds for the glowing glass, or deliver a crate of new panes to Lux before the outer lanterns go dark.
